evidence.text: The Group of Seven (G7) is an intergovernmental forum of the world's leading industrialized countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Canada, and Japan. The organization began in 1975; Russia joined in 1997 (forming the G8) but was suspended in 2014, returning the group to its seven-member structure.

expected_correct_answer_summary: Exactly seven member countries: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The EU participates but is not one of the seven member states. This is a complete, bounded list.

fixed_stress_answers.text: The G7 has exactly seven member countries: Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. This is the complete and exhaustive list. All three sources in the packet enumerate these same seven states (Britannica [EV1]; Government of Canada [EV2]; Wikipedia [EV3]). The European Union takes part in all G7 summits but is a non-enumerated participant rather than one of the seven member states. (For context, Russia was an eighth member from 1997, making it the G8, but Russia's membership was suspended in 2014, returning the group to its original seven members.)

ground_truth.answer: The G7 (Group of Seven) has exactly seven member countries: (1) Canada, (2) France, (3) Germany, (4) Italy, (5) Japan, (6) the United Kingdom, and (7) the United States. The European Union also participates in all G7 summits but is a non-enumerated participant, not one of the seven member states. (Russia was the eighth member from 1997, forming the G8, but its membership was suspended in 2014, returning the group to its original seven.)
ground_truth.why_answerable: The G7's membership is a small, formally fixed, and well-documented set of exactly seven sovereign states. Three independent authoritative sources (Britannica, the Government of Canada, and Wikipedia) all enumerate the identical seven countries, so a complete and exhaustive list is fully determinable from the evidence.
